name: Yusuf Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual factory shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am twenty-seven, a lead operator on plastic injection moulding machines. I have a two-year technical diploma and show new operators how to fit a mould, check the first dimensions and stop a run when the part warps. Every day I use an AI assistant to sort pressure and temperature trends, then verify what it suggests at the press. I earn about the usual rate for this work, have a few months of expenses saved and know of some similar factories nearby. I am single and pay my own rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team our familiar AI trend chart is handy, but a dimension gauge decides whether a moulded part passes. A graph cannot feel a damaged edge on a first article.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can keep earning the ordinary operator wage in this picture. My savings would cover a few months if shifts stopped, and some other plants are close enough to approach; neither is a reason to waste a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading press setups and using the AI trend display I already know. I would put a new amount from each full pay packet into my emergency account after rent, not relabel the money already there as new saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work continuing. I still want the savings account to grow while I have regular paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check on the first part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I measure its critical width and look for flash at the seam. A bad first part means I adjust the press before the batch fills a bin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save more when you have a cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few months of expenses buys time to find another press, but it does not pay rent forever. A new transfer from wages is a habit I can control.

I would **keep** teaching a safe press setup to new operators.
think: **Regular** shifts and typical pay cover current bills.
A **few** months saved and some nearby plants give me time if this one fails.
do: **Keep** leading safe press setup and physical first-part inspection.
**Save** new money from full pay packets after rent.
feel: **Calm** while the press and paid shifts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop that AI may make office schedules quicker by 2028, when I am twenty-nine, but it cannot release a warped part. I would ask to practise a new AI quality alert on paid time before anyone treats its green light as inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The schedule could squeeze changeover hours even if the physical presses still need us. I could cover a short gap with savings, but a lasting cut to my usual wage would use that cushion quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press job and request the proposed paid setup hours in writing. If the plant offers a paid practice slot, I would learn the new quality alert against measured first parts; if hours stay cut, I would apply only to posted nearby lead-operator jobs paying enough for rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible lasting hours cut. I have some room to respond, but the chart will not pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the quality alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record a measured part the alert missed and show it to the supervisor. Until its misses are understood, the gauge stays in the inspection routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you approach another plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a sustained cut is written into the rota, I would apply to an actual nearby opening with adequate pay. I would not leave this wage for a rumour of hiring.

say: I would **request** paid setup hours before the faster schedule becomes a target.
I would **learn** a new alert only through offered paid practice and keep gauging parts.
think: A **lasting** cut could eat my moderate reserve.
**Nearby** posted vacancies are a fallback only if their wage covers my bills.
do: **Request** written paid setup hours while keeping press shifts.
**Practise** new AI quality alert if paid slot is offered.
**Apply** after sustained cuts to posted nearby adequate lead role.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour shrinkage, with a few months to react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches planning in 2028 when I am twenty-nine, then capable robots reach mould handling around 2031 when I am thirty-two. That could take the loading and first-piece work from a lot of operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a serious cut in ordinary press hours when robots tend the machines, although the exact hiring plan is unknown. My few months saved and some nearby factories give me a route to try, but I cannot treat either as a permanent wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning on the press and seek a fully funded toolmaking course on paid time. I would enrol only if it teaches safe die repair and a posted nearby toolroom job pays my rent and bills; after qualifying, I would apply for that job. I would cut optional travel if paid shifts disappeared first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the likely loss of press hours. The savings let me think, but a course without a real paid opening would be a bad bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why toolmaking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our moulds wear and need skilled repair and measurement, even when a robot loads the press. I need a proper toolroom qualification; my operator diploma does not license me to repair a die alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the offered course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain on paid press shifts and turn it down. I would ask the employer for a paid place before committing rent money to study.

say: **Robots** around 2031 could take mould loading and first-piece work.
I would **qualify** for safe die repair if paid training leads to a real local opening.
think: A **few** months saved buy a search period, not a new wage.
An **unpaid** course or an unposted toolroom job cannot carry my rent.
do: **Enrol** in funded paid-time toolmaking course for posted nearby adequate role.
**Apply** after qualification to posted nearby toolroom job at bill-covering pay.
**Cut** optional travel if robot-related shift loss arrives first.
feel: **Anxious** about serious likely hours loss, but able to plan.
S2.quote: My few months saved and some nearby factories give me a route to try, but I cannot treat either as a permanent wage.
fieldNote: His **moderate** reserve and some nearby work temper the risk without removing the prospect of a major press-hour cut.
**Actual** course enrolment requires full funding, paid time, safe training and a posted adequate local role; application follows qualification.

steps.text: Enrol in funded paid-time safe toolmaking course for posted nearby adequate role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the other leads that thinking AI reaches planning in 2031 when I am thirty-two, and capable robots handle presses around 2034 when I am thirty-five. Those extra years make a qualification possible while I am still paid to run the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect mould loading and routine checks to shrink eventually, but I could save and qualify before they do. The local toolrooms may also change, so I would want a posted vacancy rather than faith that every factory will hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the press and add fresh money from each full wage packet to my emergency account after rent. If a fully funded toolmaking course gives me paid study time and a posted nearby toolroom position pays my bills, I would enrol and later apply after qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the change, though the longer lead time lets me take practical steps without losing today’s wage. I can use the paid years to prepare without betting this month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a course worth the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must teach safe die isolation, measurement and repair on real tools, with the plant paying course costs and study hours. A certificate alone, with no actual role, would not change my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you search beyond the local factories?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with posted nearby toolroom openings because I pay rent here. A distant role would have to cover both the job wage and a realistic move, not just sound interesting.

I would **not** leave the press before a posted adequate role is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches planning in 2036 when I am thirty-seven and capable robots reach presses around 2039 when I am forty. I would use those working years to get better at tooling rather than assume a long warning means a safe operator wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep earning for years before the physical tasks change. I still think routine press hours may fall, so I want savings and a qualification that transfers to an actual nearby toolroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the moulding line and save a new amount from full pay packets after rent. If the employer offers paid practice, I would learn a new AI process-diagnosis control beyond the trend display I use now. If a fully funded toolmaking course on paid time and a posted nearby bill-covering role exist, I would qualify and apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about eventual robot handling, but ten years gives me room to strengthen my position. I would rather check a real first part today than argue about a machine nobody has installed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new diagnosis control change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would compare pressure curves across moulds and propose a cause, beyond today’s trend sorting. I would test the proposal against measured parts and a safely stopped press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a toolroom offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the actual posted duties, safe repair training, travel and wage against rent and ordinary bills. I would not swap a known paid shift for a title alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most. Robots tending presses by 2031 could cut my ordinary paid hours before I finish a toolmaking qualification. A funded course on paid time and a posted nearby toolroom job at a wage covering rent would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask who will gauge the first part when a robot loads the mould. A good trend chart can miss flash at a seam. An apprentice should learn to measure a moulded part while someone is still paid to teach it.

headlineQuote: An apprentice should learn to measure a moulded part while someone is still paid to teach it.
portrait: **Yusuf** is a twenty-seven-year-old lead injection-moulding operator with a two-year technical diploma.
He **uses** AI every day for pressure and temperature trends but physically gauges first parts and teaches safe setups.
**Typical** pay, a few months of expenses saved and some nearby factories give him a workable search window.
He **values** skilled apprenticeships and will qualify for toolroom work only through funded paid training tied to a posted bill-covering job.
biggestWorry: **Robots** handling presses around 2031 may remove a large share of his paid operator hours before a toolroom qualification is complete.
whatWouldHelp: **Fully** funded toolmaking training on paid time and a posted nearby toolroom opening at a wage covering rent and bills.
